content: Salmonellosis is an infection caused by bacteria of the genus Salmonella. The type of Salmonella most commonly associated with human infections is referred to as non-typhoidal Salmonella. This infection is typically acquired through the consumption of raw or undercooked eggs, as well as from sources such as infected poultry, cattle, contaminated egg products, milk, reptiles carrying the bacteria on their skin, and infected pet rodents. Individuals infected with Salmonella generally develop symptoms such as diarrhea, fever, vomiting, and abdominal cramps within 6 to 72 hours after exposure. In most cases, the illness resolves within 3 to 7 days, and affected individuals recover without requiring medical treatment. However, in some cases, the diarrhea can become severe enough to cause dangerous dehydration, necessitating hospitalization. In such situations, patients are treated with intravenous fluids to address dehydration, and medications may be administered to alleviate symptoms, such as reducing fever. In severe cases, the Salmonella infection can spread from the intestines to the bloodstream and subsequently to other parts of the body. If left untreated, this can result in death. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is essential in such cases. Populations at higher risk for severe illness include the elderly, infants, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Additionally, some individuals who recover from salmonellosis may later develop reactive arthritis, a condition that can have long-term, disabling effects. A rarer form of Salmonella, known as typhoidal Salmonella, can cause typhoid fever. This form is exclusively carried by humans and is typically transmitted through direct contact with the fecal matter of an infected individual. Consequently, typhoid fever is more prevalent in regions lacking adequate systems for managing human waste. In the United States, the most common Salmonella serotypes are Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Enteritidis. Salmonella has been recognized as a cause of illness for over a century, having been discovered by an American scientist named Salmon, after whom the bacteria are named. Annually, approximately 40,000 cases of salmonellosis are reported in the United States. However, because many mild cases go undiagnosed or unreported, the actual number of infections is estimated to be 30 or more times higher. Salmonellosis is more prevalent during the summer months than in winter. Children, particularly those under five years of age, are the most likely to contract salmonellosis, with their infection rate being significantly higher than that of other age groups. Young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals are also at greater risk of developing severe infections. It is estimated that around 400 people die each year in the United States due to acute salmonellosis. National surveillance for salmonellosis is conducted through public health laboratories for culture-confirmed cases and via the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS). Active laboratoryand population-based surveillance is also carried out in FoodNet sites. The causative agents of salmonellosis are gram-negative, rod-shaped bacilli belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae and the genus Salmonella. Approximately 2,000 serotypes of Salmonella are known to cause disease in humans. Transmission of Salmonella occurs through the ingestion of contaminated food or water or through contact with infected animals. The natural history of the disease includes an estimated 400 fatal cases annually, with some cases complicated by chronic arthritis. Symptoms of salmonellosis include diarrhea (which may sometimes be bloody), fever, and abdominal cramps. In severe cases, the bacteria may invade the bloodstream or other body sites, leading to potentially life-threatening complications.
